Chapter Two: How Resistance Shapes Our Lives and Choices
Once you start to see resistance for what it is, you realize it’s everywhere. It’s not just about keeping you from sitting down to write, or picking up a paintbrush. Nope—it creeps into just about every part of life, shaping your choices, your relationships, even how you see yourself.
The wild thing is, resistance is a master of disguise. It adapts to your own fears, your tender spots, showing up in ways you’d never expect.
Picture this—a musician with a dream of recording an album. Every time the chance comes up, suddenly there’s a laundry list of reasons to wait: the gear’s not good enough, the timing’s off, there’s never enough money, or support. Days turn into weeks. The dream just sits there, always a little out of reach.
Friends say, “Go for it!” but the real fight is inside.
What if it’s not just the world throwing up roadblocks? What if it’s a part of you that’s afraid to find out what happens if you actually try?
Resistance loves to dress up as practicality.
Maybe you’re a parent who thinks, “I can’t chase that passion project—I’ve got bills and kids to look after.”
Or you just graduated and take a “safe” job, promising yourself it’s only temporary, while quietly tucking away the big ambition that used to light you up.
Resistance doesn’t always shout. Sometimes, it whispers, “Just stay safe. Stay comfortable.” And your dreams get pushed a little further back.
Then there’s self-sabotage. Imagine a writer, just pages away from finishing a book, who suddenly starts picking fights or skipping meals. It’s almost like the closer you get to your goal, the more your own mind pulls you off track.
This happens so often, it’s almost predictable—the moment you’re about to make a breakthrough, resistance hits the hardest.
Some folks try to outrun it. They move to a new city, find a different job, maybe jump into a new relationship, hoping the struggle will stay behind. But resistance isn’t something you can leave on the doorstep. It follows you, adapting to whatever’s new.
For others, resistance becomes a familiar companion. It shapes the stories they tell themselves: why they never finished the novel, or started that business, or chased the big dream. Over time, these stories turn into beliefs, and the idea of change starts to feel impossible.
But every now and then, resistance gets unmasked. Think of a painter who finally picks up the brush after years of doubting, or a teacher who stops waiting for “the perfect moment” and just starts building something new. In those moments, it’s crystal clear—resistance isn’t some outside enemy. It’s a part of you that’s scared of what might happen if you grow.
Here’s something to really remember: resistance is universal. And it gets stronger the closer you get to something meaningful. That might sound a bit daunting—but it can also be freeing. It means you’re not broken, or lacking. Struggling with resistance is just part of the creative process. And beating it? That’s not a one-time thing. It’s a daily practice.
Some people find comfort in rituals or routines, carving out a little time each day to work on what matters. Others lean on a community, sharing their struggles and lifting each other up when things get tough.
What brings them together is the understanding that resistance isn’t a problem to “fix”—it’s a reality to face.
So, here’s the key takeaway: resistance loses its grip when you call it out. When you see it, name it, and refuse to let it make your choices for you, you start to take your power back.
The work might still be hard. The doubts might not disappear. But the way forward gets clearer.
Every time you write a page, record a song, or sketch out that business plan, you’re not just making progress—you’re winning a little victory against resistance.
